summary: Sample S2 is the alloy_s2 low-density nano-bainitic (nB) Al–C steel, a high-C/high-Al grade (1.10 wt.% C, 6.05 wt.% Al) that was vacuum-melted, homogenized, hot-rolled, and then austenitized at 1150 °C for 15 min and austempered at 300 °C (just above its measured Ms of 274 °C) for a bainitic transformation finish time Bt = 3600 s. The resulting αp-free microstructure consists of fine bainitic ferrite laths with retained austenite and cementite-like (Fe,M)xCy carbides, and it combines a UTS of 1590 MPa with 7.0% elongation (PSE ≈ 11,130 MPa·%). The study examines how C–Al alloying and the austempering temperature control bainitic transformation kinetics and the strength–ductility balance in these low-density steels.
composition: Alloy S2 is an Fe-based, low-density medium-to-high-Al steel with the nominal composition (wt.%) of 1.10 C, 6.05 Al, 1.03 Mn, 0.34 Si, 0.51 Mo and 0.0039 B; Ni and Ti were not deliberately added. It differs from its closest sibling S1 mainly by a ~0.1 wt.% higher C content (S1: 0.98 C) at essentially the same Al level. Design intent: Al (6.05 wt.%) is used to lower the density (approximately 1.3% density reduction per 1 wt.% Al) and to stabilize ferrite/accelerate the bainitic transformation, while Mn is deliberately limited to ~1 wt.% for the same reason; a high C content of ~1 wt.% is required to achieve full austenitization without polygonal ferrite (αp) and to keep Ms near 300 °C despite the Ms-raising Al addition. Si (0.34 wt.%) is kept low because Al also suppresses carbide precipitation; Mo (0.51 wt.%) enhances hardenability, and a small B addition (0.0039 wt.%) further improves hardenability without harming the bainitic transformation.
processing: Processing route for S2: (1) casting of steel blocks in a vacuum arc furnace; (2) homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to promote uniform composition and microstructure; (3) step-by-step hot rolling to reduce thickness to ~11 mm, followed by slow cooling in the oven; (4) precision fabrication by water jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, Washington, USA) to obtain accurate geometries while minimizing thermal distortion, giving cylindrical specimens of ∅5×10 mm³ for heat treatment; (5) austenitizing at TA = 1150 °C for 15 min with a heating rate of 10 K s⁻¹ (TA chosen above both the calculated ferrite-free temperature of 929 °C and the measured 1031 °C to reach an αp-free microstructure); (6) cooling from austenitization to the austempering temperature at 100 K s⁻¹, fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations; (7) isothermal austempering (bainitic hold) at TB = 300 °C for Bt = 3600 s after an incubation time of 130 s, followed by final cooling. S2 belongs to the fixed-1150 °C austenitization group (S1, S2, S4, S5), used so that transformation differences are attributable to composition and TB rather than to prior-austenite conditions.
microstructure: S2 develops an αp-free nano-bainitic (nB) microstructure containing three phases: fine lath/needle bainitic ferrite (bcc) with a true lamellar thickness Lt(t) = 34 nm (standard deviation 11 nm), 29% retained austenite (γr, fcc), and rounded, nucleation-driven (Fe,M)xCy carbides (cementite-like, modified by M = Si and Mo) located near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries. S2 is αp-free both at the 1050 °C benchmark and at the applied TA of 1150 °C, so no αp–austenite interfaces are present. The key phase interfaces are γr/α and carbide/(γr–α). Lattice micro-strains are similar in both phases (εγ = 0.47%, εα = 0.44%), indicating a comparatively uniform dislocation distribution. The higher austempering temperature of 350 °C (sibling condition) coarsens the laths to 68 nm with a wider spread (SD 28 nm) and raises Vγ to 34%, so lowering TB to 300 °C refines the bainite and reduces the retained-austenite fraction (incomplete-reaction character is less pronounced at 300 °C than at 350 °C).
properties: Mechanical response of S2 after TA 1150 °C / TB 300 °C, measured on ASTM E8 sub-size round tensile specimens (12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length) on a Zwick/Roell universal testing machine (250 kN load cell), specimens heat-treated in a DIL 805A dilatometer: UTS = 1590 MPa, total elongation = 7.0%, giving a product of strength and elongation (PSE) of 11,130 MPa·%; hardness = 500 HV30. These are essentially equivalent to the sibling S1 (UTS 1600 MPa, El 6.8%, PSE 10,880 MPa·%), showing that a ~0.1 wt.% C variation has a negligible effect on the overall mechanical response. At the higher TB of 350 °C the same alloy gives UTS ≈ 1380 MPa with El = 9.4% (PSE ≈ 12,970 MPa·%). Characterization techniques applied to this sample comprise dilatometry (DIL 805A, RLC–time and RLC–temperature for Ms, Bt and kinetics), light optical microscopy (6% Nital etching, αp verification), SEM/EDX (lamellar thickness and precipitate analysis), EBSD, XRD (Rietveld/ASTM E975-13 for Vγ and micro-strain), and MatCalc precipitation/equilibrium simulations.
mechanisms: Al addition (6.05 wt.%) stabilizes ferrite and accelerates the bainitic transformation, but because a high Al content reduces the austenite single-phase field and raises Ms, a high C level (~1 wt.%) is required to remain αp-free at 1150 °C while keeping Ms near 300 °C.

The ~0.1 wt.% higher C in S2 (1.10 vs 0.98 wt.% in S1) shifts the onset of bainitic transformation toward lower temperature: hence S1 transforms faster at 350 °C (Bt 1600 s) while S2 is relatively faster at 300 °C (Bt 3600 s for S2 vs 4000 s for S1), with incubation times of 130 s (S2) and 80 s (S1) at 300 °C.

Lowering the austempering temperature to 300 °C refines the bainitic ferrite lath thickness (Lt(t) = 34 nm, SD 11 nm, versus 68 nm/SD 28 nm at 350 °C) and elevates UTS while reducing elongation, so TB primarily tunes the strength–ductility trade-off via plate thickness and retained-austenite stability.

Incomplete bainitic reaction leaves about 29% retained austenite at 300 °C: as bainite forms, C partitions into the untransformed austenite and chemically stabilizes it, suppressing further transformation; this retained-austenite fraction is lower at 300 °C (29%) than at 350 °C (34%).

(Fe,M)xCy carbides form primarily during cooling from austenitization at high nucleation kinetics between ~700 °C and 1150 °C (above the austempering hold), so their formation cannot be avoided; being rounded and nucleation-driven (not spinodal) and located near γr–bainitic ferrite boundaries, they act as locally bright particles but generate no micro-voids.

Entrapment of Si (and the presence of Mo) within the (Fe,M)xCy carbide lattice during rapid cooling stabilizes the particles and suppresses void formation, giving them a negligible direct influence on the tensile properties.

The similar lattice micro-strain of both phases in S2 (εγ = 0.47%, εα = 0.44%) indicates a relatively homogeneous dislocation distribution, avoiding the strong phase-resolved strain partitioning that causes early localization and severe ductility loss (as seen in S3 at 270 °C).
Cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ from austenitization to TB suppresses intermediate phase transformations and ensures a fine bainitic transformation.
conclusions: For the S2 alloy austenitized at 1150 °C and austempered at 300 °C, the αp-free nano-bainitic microstructure (34 nm bainitic ferrite laths, 29% retained austenite, nucleation-driven (Fe,M)xCy carbides) delivers UTS = 1590 MPa at 7.0% elongation (PSE ≈ 11,130 MPa·%), essentially matching the sibling S1 despite its ~0.1 wt.% lower C, which shows that a small C variation is secondary to the Al level in setting the strength–ductility balance. Within the study's comparison, S1 and S2 form an intermediate-fast transformation group (Bt 1600–4000 s), slower than the low-alloy S5 (Bt 700–1000 s) and far faster than the high-Al S3 (Bt 14,000–43,000 s), and their (Fe,M)xCy carbides have no measurable detrimental effect on tensile behaviour because they form above the austempering temperature without micro-void formation. S2 reaches its own peak product of strength and elongation (PSE ≈ 13,000 MPa·%) at the higher TB of 350 °C, whereas the 300 °C condition trades ductility for strength. The findings reinforce that C–Al composition and the austempering temperature are the pivotal levers governing bainitic transformation kinetics and the resulting strength–ductility response in low-density nano-bainitic steels.
unmapped: Because S1 and S2 differ only negligibly, the MatCalc TTP diagram calculated for S1 (T_A 1150 °C, with TB 350 °C/Bt 2300 s and TB 300 °C/Bt 3600 s) is taken as approximately representative of S2.

Ms of S2 measured by the tangent-intersection method on RLC–T cooling curves is 274 °C after 1150 °C austenitization; the operational/measured austenitizing temperature of S2 was 1031 °C and the calculated ferrite-free TA was 929 °C.

The bainitic transformation finish time Bt was defined as the point where the transformation rate dropped to a negligible level, corresponding to the onset of the plateau in the RLC curve; this definition carries some subjective interpretation but is expected to have negligible effect on final properties.
S2 was already αp-free at the 1050 °C benchmark temperature, consistent with its lower derivative-based austenitizing temperature, and remained αp-free at the applied TA of 1150 °C.
S2 is not Ti-microalloyed and contains no Ni; consequently the TiMoC-related suppression of (Fe,M)xCy reported for S4 does not apply to this sample.
